title: Joining the Oceans and the Continent, 1869
subtitle: The Pacific Railroad at Promontory Summit and the Suez Canal opening, 1854–1869
intro: In 1869 two pieces of the world's transport map were joined six months apart. On 10 May at Promontory Summit, Utah, the Central Pacific building east from Sacramento met the Union Pacific building west from Omaha, and a telegraph operator sent one word across the country. On 17 November the Empress Eugénie's yacht L'Aigle led some forty ships into the Suez Canal, and three days later the procession reached the Red Sea. A continent had been crossed by rail and two oceans by a ditch through the desert.

The honest record of both is mostly not diaries. It is company letters and payrolls, chief engineers' reports, dated photographs, speeches as the newspapers printed them, a crown prince's privately printed travel diary, a painter's notebook, and a poet's verse letter written a year later. Where that is the form of the source, the entries say so. Several eyes are institutions or collective records rather than single diarists.

Both works were built by labour that left almost no words of its own. The Central Pacific's workforce was overwhelmingly Chinese, perhaps ten thousand or more men at its height; they appear in payrolls as 'China Men', in newspapers as numbers, and at Promontory only at the edges of the photographs, though a Chinese gang laid the last rail. The Suez Canal's first channel was dug by Egyptian peasants conscripted under the corvée until Napoleon III's arbitration ended the system in 1864; how many died is contested, from the 120,000 of Nasser's 1956 speech to historians who say no archive supports that figure. Both are traced here through the records that kept them, and the gaps are stated.

The ledger of trials runs from concession to opening: the strike of 1867, the ten miles and 56 feet laid by hand on 28 April 1869, the disputed mileages of the final spike, the joining of the seas in August, and a British survey ship said to have slipped ahead of the Empress in the dark. Distances, depths and dates are given as the record gives them, with rival figures shown side by side.

Read together, the two openings show the same pattern from different sides of the world: owners and engineers who spoke of commerce with Asia and India, photographers and painters who composed the official image, a press that counted miles and dividends, and workers who appear only when someone else wrote them down.
calendar_note: All dates are Gregorian. Egyptian official documents of the time were also dated in the Islamic (Hijri) calendar, and Ottoman usage applied in some correspondence, but the canal company, the guests and the press used the Gregorian calendar. Promontory times are local; the telegraph times reported in eastern cities differ by the time zone.

eyes.name: Grenville Mellen Dodge
eyes.role: Chief engineer of the Union Pacific Railroad, aged 38; former Union major general
eyes.where: Omaha and the UP line across Wyoming and Utah; Promontory Summit on 10 May
eyes.form: official reports, dated telegrams and a memoir (written later)
eyes.authenticity: Dodge's papers are at the State Historical Society of Iowa. His chief engineer's reports were printed by the company; his best-known narrative, How We Built the Union Pacific Railway, was printed as a US Senate document in 1910, forty years after the event, and is a memoir that defends his own role. Entries drawn from it are marked approx.
eyes.bio: A railroad surveyor turned Civil War general who rebuilt Union railroads in the West and South, Dodge ran the UP's location and construction from 1866. At Promontory he lost the argument over who would drive the last spike. His record is the engineer's and the soldier's: distances, grades, contests won.

sources.title: Meeting at Promontory Point (summary of the 10 May programme, citing Dodge)

eyes.name: Leland Stanford
eyes.role: President of the Central Pacific Railroad, aged 45; former governor of California
eyes.where: Sacramento; the CP special train to Promontory
eyes.vantage_label: the Central Pacific's president and ceremonial spike-driver
eyes.form: dated letters; speech as printed in the press
eyes.authenticity: Stanford's business letters to his partners (Hopkins, Huntington, Crocker) survive in company and Stanford University collections and are cited by the Chinese Railroad Workers in North America Project. His Promontory speech survives only as the newspapers printed it, with small differences between versions.
eyes.bio: One of the Central Pacific's 'Big Four', Stanford brought the gold and silver spikes and the silver-plated maul to Promontory. His letters show an impatient owner watching costs and mileage; his public words framed the line as a road to Asian trade. His company's workforce was mostly Chinese, a fact his ceremony barely showed.

sources.title: Chinese Railroad Workers in North America Project: timeline (Stanford to Hopkins, 15 Jan 1869)

eyes.name: Samuel Benedict Reed
eyes.role: Union Pacific superintendent of construction, aged about 50
eyes.where: UP end-of-track camps at Echo and Weber, Utah; Boston in August 1869
eyes.vantage_label: the builder at end of track, writing home
eyes.form: dated letters to his wife and family
eyes.authenticity: Reed's letters are in the Samuel Reed Papers, Nebraska State History (History Nebraska), and are transcribed by the University of Nebraska's Railroads and the Making of Modern America project. A family compiler added celebratory notes that the project itself flags as not entirely accurate; those notes are not used here as Reed's words.
eyes.bio: Reed ran the day-to-day building of the UP across Wyoming and Utah. His letters home are the most candid UP record of the last winter: snow blockades, missing ties, and repeated anger at Thomas Durant's interference and spending. After the spike he spent August in Boston answering the board's questions about where the money went.

eyes.name: Charles Roscoe Savage
eyes.role: Salt Lake City photographer, aged 37; English-born Latter-day Saint convert
eyes.where: Salt Lake City; Promontory Summit on 10 May
eyes.vantage_label: a local photographer at the gap
eyes.authenticity: Savage kept diaries for much of his life; they are held with his papers at Brigham Young University and have been quoted by historians of the ceremony. Their exact wording for 10 May could not be checked for this chapter, so entries rely on the dated photographs, which survive at BYU, Utah State University and the Church History Library.
eyes.bio: Savage came to Promontory from Salt Lake City and photographed the crowd and engines alongside the railroads' own photographers. As a Utah resident he saw the line arriving into a territory that had supplied grading contracts and crews for both companies. His plates are among the few that show the workers gathered before the spike.

sources.title: C. R. Savage Collection, BYU (about)
Savage, Golden Spike Ceremony at Promontory, 10 May 1869 (USU A-0860)

eyes.name: Andrew Joseph Russell
eyes.role: Official photographer to the Union Pacific, aged 39; former captain and photographer of the US Military Railroad Construction Corps
eyes.where: Along the UP line; Promontory Summit on 10 May
eyes.authenticity: About 650 of Russell's 10 x 13 inch glass-plate negatives are held by the Oakland Museum of California. The Promontory plates are dated to 10 May 1869 by the event itself. They are a deliberate, posed record; the Central Pacific's photographer Alfred A. Hart and Savage worked the same day.
eyes.bio: Russell learned to photograph railroads in war, recording Herman Haupt's military railroad crews. For the UP he made the most famous image of the day, the two locomotives nose to nose with the engineers' champagne bottles raised. Wet-plate exposure meant the crowd had to hold still, and the composition shows whom the companies wanted seen.

sources.title: NPS Golden Spike: A Moment in Time (Russell)
Russell, Salsbury's Cut, Promontory (Oakland Museum H69.459.2409)

eyes.name: Chinese workers of the Central Pacific (payrolls and press)
eyes.role: Some 10,000 or more labourers, foremen, cooks, masons and headmen, mostly from Guangdong; numbers rose and fell by season
eyes.where: Sierra Nevada tunnels and camps; Nevada and Utah grades; Victory/Rozel camp near Promontory
eyes.vantage_label: the builders, traced through company records
eyes.form: company payroll records; press reports; later commemoration (no first-person diaries survive)
eyes.authenticity: No diaries or letters by Central Pacific Chinese workers are known to survive in the US or China. They appear in CP payroll sheets (often as 'China Men' or by camp and headman), company letters and newspapers that rarely give names. The Chinese Railroad Workers in North America Project at Stanford has digitised payrolls from the California State Railroad Museum. Numbers are estimates; the toll of deaths is not accurately known (the NPS cites estimates of over a thousand).
eyes.bio: This eye stands for the people who did most of the Central Pacific's work and left almost none of its paper. They struck in 1867 for higher pay and shorter tunnel shifts, laid most of the ten miles of 28 April 1869, and set the last rail at Promontory. Their foreman Hung Wah is one of the few named in the record of that day.

sources.title: Chinese Railroad Workers in North America Project: timeline
'China Men', CPRR Payroll No. 158, May 1865 (Stanford project)
NPS: Chinese Labor and the Iron Road

eyes.name: San Francisco, Sacramento and Salt Lake newspapers
eyes.role: Daily Alta California, Sacramento Union, San Francisco Bulletin, Salt Lake Telegram and their correspondents
eyes.where: San Francisco, Sacramento, Salt Lake City; correspondents at end of track
eyes.vantage_label: the regional press, counting and cheering
eyes.authenticity: Dated newspaper columns, cited here through the Stanford project timeline and the Railroads and the Making of Modern America transcription of the Salt Lake Telegram (11 May 1869). Papers were friendly to the companies and gave mileages that do not always agree with each other.
eyes.bio: The papers were the railroad's scoreboard: they counted workers, miles and days, printed the company figures, and staged the celebrations. They also preserve most of what is known of the Chinese crews, usually as numbers. Their figures for the final distances differ, and both versions are kept here.

sources.title: Salt Lake Telegram, 11 May 1869, in the Samuel Reed Papers
Stanford project timeline (Alta, Union, Bulletin citations)

eyes.name: Ferdinand de Lesseps
eyes.role: Former French diplomat, aged 64; founder and president of the Compagnie universelle du canal maritime de Suez
eyes.where: Paris, Ismailia and Port Said; aboard the procession 17–20 November
eyes.form: dated letters, journal and documents (published by himself)
eyes.authenticity: Lesseps published his own correspondence and journal as Lettres, journal et documents pour servir à l'histoire du canal de Suez (5 vols, Paris, 1875–81), a selection made to defend the enterprise. His speeches at the opening survive through the press. Dates for the events are confirmed by the Riou album and contemporary papers.
eyes.bio: Not an engineer but a diplomat with Egyptian connections, Lesseps obtained the concession in 1854 and kept the project alive through British hostility and the end of forced labour. His record is the promoter's: triumph, shareholders and France's prestige. The Egyptians whose labour dug the first channel appear in it as a problem of supply.

sources.title: Hérodote: l'inauguration du canal de Suez
Fondation Napoléon: Riou, Inauguration ceremony at Port Said

eyes.name: Friedrich Wilhelm, Crown Prince of Prussia (later Emperor Frederick III)
eyes.role: Heir to the Prussian throne, aged 37, representing his father King Wilhelm at the opening
eyes.where: Constantinople, the Holy Land, Egypt; the opening flotilla
eyes.authenticity: His Tagebuch meiner Reise nach dem Morgenlande 1869 was privately printed for family and friends; a dedicated copy with a bound-in map survives in the Geheimes Staatsarchiv Preußischer Kulturbesitz (VI. HA, FA Buttlar-Venedien, Nr. 3). The wording of individual days could not be consulted for this chapter, so entries record only his documented presence and are marked approx.
eyes.bio: The future Frederick III travelled east for some six weeks and kept a diary he later had printed. He sailed in the flotilla behind L'Aigle and sat at the Khedive's supper at Ismailia. Within a year he would command an army against the France whose Empress led the procession.

sources.title: GStA PK record: Tagebuch meiner Reise nach dem Morgenlande 1869
Riou, Le souper des souverains à Ismaïlia (caption names the Prussian Crown Prince)

eyes.name: Henrik Ibsen
eyes.role: Norwegian playwright, aged 41, living in Dresden; invited by the Khedive as Norway's representative
eyes.where: Cairo, the Nile to Aswan, Port Said and the canal
eyes.form: poem-letter (written a year later) and letters
eyes.authenticity: Ibsen kept no diary of the trip. His fullest account is the verse letter Ballonbrev til en svensk dame (Balloon Letter to a Swedish Lady), written in Dresden in December 1870 during the siege of Paris and printed in Digte (1871); it recalls Egypt and the canal through the lens of the Franco-Prussian war. His letters are edited in Henrik Ibsens skrifter (University of Oslo).
eyes.bio: Ibsen was among the European writers the Khedive shipped up the Nile before the opening. While he was away his comedy The League of Youth opened in Christiania. His later poem turns the pharaohs and the canal festivities into a warning about the new German militarism, a reading back of 1869 through 1870.

sources.title: University of Oslo: chronological survey of Ibsen's life (1869, 1870)
GHDI: Henrik Ibsen's Balloon Letter, December 1870

eyes.name: Eugène Fromentin
eyes.role: French painter and writer, aged 49, one of the Khedive's invited French guests
eyes.where: Marseille, Cairo, the Nile expedition, the canal
eyes.authenticity: Fromentin's manuscript carnet of the 1869 trip was edited by Jean-Marie Carré as Voyage en Égypte (1869): journal publié d'après le carnet manuscrit (Paris: Montaigne/Aubier, 1935). Because the edition was first published after 1928, no quotation is used. Exact entry dates are given here only where the expedition's own itinerary confirms them.
eyes.bio: A painter of Algeria and a fine prose writer (Dominique, 1863), Fromentin treated the trip as a painter's working notebook: light, colour and the flatness of the river, rather than ceremony. He travelled with the official expedition up the Nile. His view is that of a guest whose real interest lay outside the programme.

sources.title: ARCE Library record: Voyage en Égypte (1869), ed. Carré, 1935
La gran expedición al Alto Egipto (itinerary of the Khedive's guests)

eyes.name: Théophile Gautier
eyes.role: French poet and critic, aged 58, invited in the Empress's escort of writers
eyes.where: At sea, then confined in Cairo
eyes.vantage_label: the invited guest who missed it
eyes.authenticity: Gautier's account appeared in the Journal officiel in 1870 and was collected after his death in L'Orient (1877). It is a written-up account, not a diary. Louise Colet, another guest, described his accident in Les Pays lumineux (1879).
eyes.bio: Gautier had written about the Orient for thirty years without going to Egypt. On the voyage out he broke his arm, and spent most of the trip watching Cairo from a hotel terrace while the others went up the Nile and to the canal. His record is of a celebration seen from a sickroom.

sources.title: BnF Bibliothèques d'Orient: Théophile Gautier

eyes.name: Egyptian fellahin of the corvée (company, state and later records)
eyes.role: Peasant labourers conscripted in rotation, usually for about a month at a time, to dig the first canal channels
eyes.side: Egyptian peasantry; conscripted by the Egyptian state for the Suez Company
eyes.where: The isthmus between Port Said, Lake Timsah and the Bitter Lakes
eyes.vantage_label: the diggers, barely in the record
eyes.form: company and official records; later historiography and political speech (no first-person accounts)
eyes.authenticity: No diaries or letters by corvée labourers are known. They appear as numbers in Suez Company and Egyptian government correspondence, in British criticism of the system, and in the 1864 arbitration. Death figures are contested: 120,000 is the figure cited by President Nasser in 1956; historians such as Caroline Piquet (CNRS) say no reliable archive supports it, while still allowing for heavy losses. Both positions are given; neither is adopted here.
eyes.bio: This eye stands for the Egyptian peasants who dug by hand before the dredgers came. They were called up under the old duty to clear the Nile channels, moved in rotation into the desert, and then withdrawn after 1864 when foreign workers and steam dredgers took over. They are present at the opening only as an absence.

sources.title: CNRS News: the Suez Canal, a history (interview with Caroline Piquet)

eyes.name: The Spectator and the London press
eyes.role: London weekly and daily papers reporting the opening by telegraph
eyes.authenticity: The Spectator's paragraph of 20 November 1869 survives in its digitised archive. It was written from early telegrams and dates the opening to the 18th. The story of HMS Newport slipping ahead of L'Aigle comes from later naval accounts and is marked approx.
eyes.bio: British governments had opposed the canal for fifteen years, and the London papers covered its opening with interest in tolls and the route to India rather than in ceremony. The Spectator's first word is a sceptical one about dividends. It stands for the view from the country whose shipping would soon dominate the canal.

sources.title: The Spectator, 20 November 1869
Dawlish Chronicles: HMS Newport at the opening

entries.headline: A 99-year concession for a canal through the isthmus
entries.digest: Lesseps, an old friend of the new viceroy Said, obtained the concession to cut a maritime canal across the isthmus of Suez. The company would hold it for 99 years after opening. British opposition, money and labour were all still to be found.
entries.source_note: Hérodote dossier (concession of 25 Nov 1854); Lesseps, Lettres, journal et documents, vol. 1.

entries.headline: Called up from the villages to dig by hand
entries.digest: Under the old duty to keep the Nile channels clear, the Egyptian state sent peasants into the desert in rotation, about a month at a time, to dig the first channel for the company. The CNRS account puts the number mobilised at about 400,000 over the corvée years. Water, food and disease were constant problems in camps far from the river. None of the diggers is known to have left a written word.
entries.source_note: CNRS News (Piquet interview): about 400,000 fellahs mobilised; the article dates the mobilisation 1859–1862. Rotation of about a month from the same source.

entries.headline: Napoleon III's arbitration ends the corvée on the canal
entries.digest: After British protests and Ottoman pressure halted the work, Napoleon III acted as arbiter between the company and Egypt. Egypt withdrew the conscripted labour and paid the company a large indemnity for its loss. Foreign workers from Greece, Italy and Dalmatia, and above all steam dredgers, took over the digging.
entries.source_note: CNRS News (arbitration; foreign labour; mechanisation). Month of the award from standard histories; not checked to the day.

entries.headline: 'China Men' on the payroll
entries.digest: A Central Pacific payroll for May 1865 lists its Chinese gangs under the heading 'China Men', grouped by camp and headman rather than by individual name. The Sacramento Union counted about 2,000 men on the line that spring, two-thirds of them Chinese, and payrolls show over 3,000 Chinese employed by March–May. These sheets are among the few documents where the workers appear at all.
entries.source_note: CPRR Payroll No. 158, May 1865 (Stanford project image); Stanford project timeline, spring 1865.

entries.place: Sierra summit tunnels, Cisco to Truckee
entries.headline: Several thousand strike for pay and shorter shifts
entries.digest: Chinese workers along about thirty miles of the line stopped work, asking for $40 a month instead of $35 and shorter hours, especially in the tunnels. Crocker and Strobridge cut off the food and supply trains to the camps. After about a week the strike ended without a raise.
entries.source_note: Stanford project timeline (June 1867); NPS Chinese Labor and the Iron Road (Cisco–Truckee, about a week).

entries.headline: Crocker reports the gangs back at work
entries.digest: Charles Crocker reported that all but one or two gangs had returned to work with no change in pay. The company's record of the strike is its own: it gives the management's terms and none of the strikers' words.
entries.source_note: Stanford project timeline, 3 July 1867 (Crocker report).

entries.headline: Thirty-nine boxes of remains bound for China
entries.digest: A schooner arriving at San Francisco carried 39 boxes of the remains of Chinese who had died, to be sent home to China for burial. The press noted it in passing. It is one of the few traces in print of the deaths among the workers, whose total no one counted.
entries.source_note: Stanford project timeline, 15 Dec 1868.

entries.headline: Durant 'retards the work', Reed tells his wife
entries.digest: Reed wrote home that money had poured out over the past two months and that Thomas Durant, the UP vice-president camped at Echo, was alarmed at the bills he himself was causing. In Reed's view every month Durant stayed cost the company hundreds of thousands of dollars and slowed the track. He had two letters from home still unanswered.
entries.source_note: Reed to family, 12 Jan 1869 (railroads.unl.edu rail.reed.0104).

entries.headline: Stanford complains the road east of Ogden is slow
entries.digest: Writing to his partner Mark Hopkins, Stanford complained that progress on the grading from Ogden toward Monument was too slow. The race with the Union Pacific for Utah mileage, and the government bonds per mile that came with it, was now the whole game.
entries.source_note: Stanford project timeline, 15 Jan 1869 (Stanford to Hopkins).

entries.headline: Valley people see their first railway
entries.digest: Track had reached Weber the previous Thursday, and crowds came every day to see the cars; for many in the valley it was the first railway they had ever seen. Reed spent most of his letter on Durant: in October he had pulled the teams and half the graders onto distributing ties, the ground froze, and earth that cost thirty cents a yard to move now had to be blasted at night. Reed feared a financial crash.
entries.source_note: Reed to family, 16 Jan 1869 (rail.reed.0105).

entries.headline: Irish UP graders attack Chinese CP crews
entries.digest: Where the two companies' grades ran side by side in Utah, Irish Union Pacific workers threw frozen clods at Chinese Central Pacific crews, and later raids and blasting followed. After the Central Pacific complained, the UP ordered its men to stop. The record comes from company and press sources, not from either set of workers.
entries.source_note: Stanford project timeline, 22 Feb 1869.

entries.headline: Snow blockade: four weeks without a letter
entries.digest: A snow blockade had cut the mails from the East, and Reed had gone over four weeks without a letter from home. Track was past Devil's Gate and grading done forty miles ahead, but ties were short and supplies would run out if the storms lasted twenty more days. He expected grading done within sixty days and longed for a year's rest.
entries.source_note: Reed to family, 27 Feb 1869 (rail.reed.0108).

entries.headline: Promontory fixed as the meeting point
entries.digest: After months in which the two companies graded past each other across Utah, Dodge and the Central Pacific's Collis Huntington agreed on a meeting point at Promontory Summit, and Congress confirmed it by joint resolution on 10 April. Dodge later told the story as a hard-won settlement of an absurd duplication of work.
entries.source_note: Joint resolution of 10 Apr 1869 cited in NPS Golden Spike cultural landscape report; Dodge, How We Built the Union Pacific (1910) for his account.

entries.headline: Ten miles and 56 feet in twelve hours
entries.digest: Following a bet with the Union Pacific, the Central Pacific's mixed crews laid ten miles and 56 feet of track between dawn and dusk, a record never beaten by hand. At least 400 Chinese workers levelled, laid ties, spiked and bolted; eight Irish rail handlers lifted the iron, and later accounts name them as Shay, Kennedy, Sullivan, Joyce, Daley, Wyatt, Killeen and McNamara. The Chinese workers were not named.
entries.source_note: Stanford project timeline, 28 Apr 1869 (10 miles 56 ft, 12 hours); NPS Chinese Labor and the Iron Road (400 Chinese; eight Irish rail handlers). Irish names from later accounts, not checked against a payroll.

entries.headline: The Bulletin crows over the ten-mile day
entries.digest: The San Francisco Bulletin hailed the day's work in the most extravagant terms the paper could find. An army officer watching was reported telling Crocker he had never seen such organisation. Neither report named a single Chinese worker.
entries.quote: the greatest work in tracklaying ever accomplished or conceived
entries.source_note: Stanford project timeline, 28 Apr 1869 (Bulletin quotation). Exact issue date not checked.

entries.headline: 557 Chinese workers waiting to move on
entries.digest: A Daily Alta correspondent described 557 Chinese workers at Rosebud, their grading finished, about to be sent north for other railroad work. With the junction days away, the workforce was already being dispersed.
entries.source_note: Stanford project timeline, 5 May 1869 (Daily Alta).

entries.headline: The ceremony is postponed
entries.digest: The papers reported that the joining set for 8 May was put off to the 10th because rains had washed out Union Pacific track in Weber Canyon. Behind it lay a less public delay: on 6 May at Piedmont, Wyoming, unpaid workers held Thomas Durant's special car until wages were wired from New York. Sacramento and San Francisco, already committed, began celebrating on the 8th anyway.
entries.source_note: Meeting at Promontory Point essay (rains; Piedmont hostage of 6 May); California celebrations of 8 May from standard accounts.

entries.headline: A fight in the Chinese camp, settled by Strobridge
entries.digest: A violent clash broke out between rival factions in the Chinese camp at Victory, two days before the ceremony. The CP construction boss James Strobridge put it down. The record gives the company's intervention and nothing of the cause as the workers saw it.
entries.source_note: Stanford project timeline, 8 May 1869.

entries.headline: A Chinese gang lays the last rail
entries.digest: Around midday a Chinese work gang laid the last ties and rails across the gap before the officials took over with the ceremonial spikes. Afterwards the foreman Hung Wah and other Chinese workers were invited to a reception in Strobridge's private car and cheered there. In the public ceremony and most of the photographs they are hard to find.
entries.source_note: Stanford project timeline, 10 May 1869 (Hung Wah; Strobridge's car); NPS (Chinese contingent present).

entries.headline: Stanford speaks, swings and misses
entries.digest: Stanford had agreed the programme with Durant only minutes before. In his speech he spoke for the Central Pacific of the line as a highway for the commerce of Asia and the nation. Then he and Durant swung at the precious spikes with the silver-plated maul and missed, to the crowd's delight; an ordinary iron spike wired to the telegraph closed the circuit.
entries.source_note: Meeting at Promontory Point essay (programme; missed blows). Speech content from press versions, which differ slightly.

entries.headline: Dodge loses the spike and speaks of the road to India
entries.digest: Dodge had pressed for the UP to drive the last spike and lost the argument to Stanford's programme. Speaking for the Union Pacific, he recalled Thomas Hart Benton's old dream of a route to India across the continent and declared it realised. He shook hands with the CP's chief engineer Samuel Montague beside the locomotives.
entries.source_note: Meeting at Promontory Point essay (dispute over the spike); NPS Moment in Time (Montague and Dodge handshake); Dodge's remarks as printed in the press and his 1910 memoir.

entries.headline: East and West shaking hands
entries.digest: Russell set up his camera before UP No. 119 and the CP's Jupiter, run forward until their pilots almost touched. Engineers George Booth and Sam Bradford broke champagne on each other's engines, and Montague and Dodge shook hands in the middle. With no shutter, Russell uncapped the lens and counted, and the crowd had to stand still for the exposure.
entries.source_note: NPS Golden Spike, A Moment in Time (Russell; engines; champagne; handshake; wet-plate method).

entries.headline: A Salt Lake photographer works the crowd
entries.digest: Savage came up from Salt Lake City and photographed the gathering at the gap, including railroad workers grouped by the nearly finished line before the golden spike. About a thousand people were there, nearly all men, with soldiers of the 21st Infantry and a few women and children. He worked alongside Russell and the Central Pacific's photographer Alfred Hart.
entries.source_note: USU Special Collections A-0860 (Savage, workers gathered before the spike, dated 10 May 1869); NPS Moment in Time (crowd); diary wording not checked.

entries.headline: 'DONE'
entries.digest: At about 12:20 local time the operator W. N. Shilling warned the lines to stand by, and at about 12:45 he tapped out the single word. Chicago staged a parade some seven miles long, New York fired salutes and Wall Street closed, the bells of Independence Hall rang in Philadelphia, and San Francisco celebrated far into the night.
entries.source_note: Meeting at Promontory Point essay (times; 'Done'; celebrations).

entries.headline: The Salt Lake Telegram tallies the road
entries.digest: The next day's Salt Lake Telegram reported a day without accident and rival crews meeting in peace. It placed the last rail 1,084½ miles west of Omaha and 690 miles east of Sacramento, listed the gold spike from California and the silver from Nevada, and gave a cost of over $100 million. A copy of the account survives among the UP superintendent Samuel Reed's papers.
entries.source_note: Salt Lake Telegram, 11 May 1869, in the Samuel Reed Papers (rail.reed.0109).

entries.headline: Two days before the board: who spent the money?
entries.digest: Three months after the spike, Reed was in Boston being questioned by the Union Pacific directors about the enormous sums spent in the past year. He expected them to blame the company itself for giving supreme command to one man, meaning Durant, and hoped to be credited for trying to hold costs down. A tie contractor's lawsuit was still pending.
entries.source_note: Reed to family, 7 Aug 1869 (rail.reed.0111).

entries.headline: The two seas meet
entries.digest: Water from the Mediterranean and the Red Sea was let together in the canal, three months before the opening. The cut ran about 162 kilometres, and the company was dredging to a working depth of about eight metres. Much of the remaining spoil had been moved by steam dredgers, not by hand.
entries.source_note: Hérodote dossier (waters joined 15 Aug 1869; 162 km, 8 m depth).

entries.headline: Defending the tie contractor; Dodge expected
entries.digest: Reed laid out for Oakes Ames and his associates why the contractor Davis deserved to be paid: Durant had ordered ties and timber, then taken Davis's teams away, so stockpiles lay buried in snow and new ties had to be cut. Ties floated down the Laramie and Green rivers had been stranded by low water. Dodge was expected in Boston that evening.
entries.source_note: Reed to family, 17 Aug 1869 (rail.reed.0114).

entries.headline: The Khedive's guests embark on the Moeris
entries.digest: The first group of invited French guests sailed from Marseille on the Messageries Impériales steamer Moeris for Alexandria, then went on by rail to Cairo to wait for the rest. Fromentin was among the French writers and artists invited. He brought a notebook rather than an easel.
entries.source_note: La gran expedición al Alto Egipto (itinerary: 7 Oct Paris, 9 Oct Moeris); Fromentin's presence in the first group assumed from his place on the Nile expedition.

entries.headline: Gautier breaks his arm
entries.digest: On the passage to Egypt the poet fell and broke his arm. It confined him for most of the trip. The man who had written about the Orient for decades would see Egypt chiefly from his Cairo hotel.
entries.source_note: BnF Bibliothèques d'Orient (broke his arm at sea; confined); day not known.

entries.headline: The League of Youth opens at home while he is away
entries.digest: While Ibsen waited in Cairo with the other guests, his new comedy The League of Youth had its first performance at the Christiania Theatre, to a stormy reception from those who saw themselves satirised. He heard of it by letter weeks later, far up the Nile.
entries.source_note: University of Oslo chronology (1869: League of Youth published and first performed; Egypt). Premiere day from standard Ibsen chronologies.

entries.headline: Up the Nile with the expedition
entries.digest: About 150 guests left Cairo on four small steamers for a fortnight's voyage to Aswan, stopping at Luxor, Karnak, Edfu and Philae, under the archaeological direction of Auguste Mariette's service. Fromentin's carnet from the voyage is a painter's: the colour of banks and water, the light at different hours, the problem of rendering so flat a land.
entries.source_note: Expedition itinerary (22 Oct; ~150 guests; four steamers); character of the carnet from Carré's edition as described in its catalogue and studies. No quotation (published 1935).

entries.headline: Ibsen sails south among the writers
entries.digest: Ibsen was among the writers listed on the Khedive's Nile expedition, sailing with French, German and other guests toward Aswan and the temples. The voyage gave him the pharaohs, temples and the desert that a year later furnished his poem-letter.
entries.source_note: Expedition itinerary (Ibsen named among the writers); departure day from the itinerary, not from Ibsen's own record.

entries.headline: Watching Cairo from a hotel terrace
entries.digest: While the other guests sailed up the Nile and then went to the canal, Gautier stayed in Cairo with his arm set, watching the city from the terrace of his hotel. The articles he wrote afterwards are built from that view and from what others told him.
entries.source_note: BnF Bibliothèques d'Orient (confined to watching Cairo from his hotel terrace).

entries.headline: Blessings on the beach at Port Said
entries.digest: With the Empress Eugénie newly arrived, the inauguration began at Port Said with religious ceremonies on grandstands by the shore, Muslim and Christian clergy each blessing the work. Warships of many nations lay in the roads. For Lesseps it was the vindication of fifteen years of struggle.
entries.source_note: Fondation Napoléon (16 Nov, Port Said religious ceremonies; Eugénie's arrival); The Spectator, 20 Nov 1869 (Muslim and Catholic prayers).

entries.headline: The Crown Prince among the sovereigns
entries.digest: The Prussian heir, arriving from his tour of Constantinople and the Holy Land, joined the Emperor Franz Joseph, the Empress Eugénie and the Khedive Ismail at the Port Said ceremonies. His printed diary of the journey covers these days.
entries.source_note: Fondation Napoléon (guests); GStA PK record of the printed Tagebuch. Diary text not consulted.

entries.headline: HMS Newport slips ahead of L'Aigle
entries.digest: According to later naval accounts, Commander George Nares took the survey ship HMS Newport through the waiting ships in darkness, without lights, and placed her in front of the French imperial yacht. At dawn the French found a British ship first in line, in a channel too narrow to pass. Nares was officially reprimanded and privately thanked, and promoted captain that year.
entries.source_note: Dawlish Chronicles (secondary; no references given). Not checked against the ship's log or Admiralty papers.

entries.headline: L'Aigle leads the procession into the canal
entries.digest: At the cannon signal the imperial yacht L'Aigle, carrying the Empress and Lesseps, led some forty ships into the canal: the Khedive, the Emperor of Austria, the Crown Prince of Prussia, the princes of the Netherlands and Hanover, the British and Russian ambassadors. By evening L'Aigle was at anchor in Lake Timsah off Ismailia, the company's new town halfway down the isthmus.
entries.source_note: Fondation Napoléon (17 Nov; about 40 ships; L'Aigle at Ismailia that evening).

entries.place: Aboard the Prussian flotilla, Port Said to Ismailia
entries.headline: Behind the Empress's yacht
entries.digest: The Crown Prince's vessel followed L'Aigle and the Khedive's yacht in the procession into the canal. His diary records the first day's passage to Lake Timsah. The order of ships was itself a matter of national standing.
entries.source_note: Fondation Napoléon (Crown Prince in flotilla); GStA PK diary record. Diary text not consulted.

entries.headline: Present at the opening
entries.digest: Back from the Nile, Ibsen was among the guests at the opening of the canal. In the poem he wrote a year later he recalled the ships and flags of the nations on the canal, set against the silence of the old Egypt he had just seen.
entries.source_note: University of Oslo chronology (present at the opening); content of recollection from the Balloon Letter (1870).

entries.headline: At the Khedive's supper and ball
entries.digest: Ismail gave a supper and ball at Ismailia for thousands of guests. Riou's picture made for Lesseps names the Prussian Crown Prince among those at the sovereigns' table, with Franz Joseph, Eugénie, the Dutch prince and princess, the Khedive and Lesseps. The cost of such hospitality would help push Egypt into debt within a few years.
entries.source_note: Riou, Le souper des souverains à Ismaïlia (Fondation Napoléon; 18 Nov; guests named).

entries.headline: A desert town lit for a ball
entries.digest: Lesseps's town on Lake Timsah, a few years earlier a workers' camp, received the sovereigns and several thousand guests. The supper and ball given by the Khedive were the social summit of the festivities, recorded for Lesseps in Riou's watercolours. Some sixty French guests were among those invited by the Khedive.
entries.source_note: Riou/Fondation Napoléon (supper and ball, 18 Nov; thousands; 60 French guests invited).

entries.headline: The procession reaches the Red Sea
entries.digest: After passing the Bitter Lakes, the leading ships arrived at Suez, completing the first ceremonial transit. Lesseps had made his point that steamships could pass from sea to sea. Deeper-draught ships would take longer: the Spanish frigate Berenguela had to lighten ship and did not reach Suez until 17 December.
entries.source_note: Riou album covering 16–20 Nov (Fondation Napoléon); Berenguela from the Spanish expedition article.

entries.headline: The Spectator: opened, but will it pay?
entries.digest: The Spectator reported the opening in a few lines, dating it to the 18th from early telegrams. It noted the Russian steamer, L'Aigle and about forty small steamers, the prayers of imams and priests, and Lesseps's speech attacking France's resistance to reforming the capitulations. It doubted that tolls of ten francs a ton would give shareholders much, and said the canal would need deepening and passing places.
entries.source_note: The Spectator, 20 Nov 1869, p. 1.

entries.headline: The trip written up for the Journal officiel
entries.digest: Gautier published his account of the journey in the Journal officiel in 1870, months before the fall of the Empire whose Empress had led the procession. The pieces were collected after his death in L'Orient (1877). They describe an Egypt seen largely at second hand.
entries.source_note: BnF Bibliothèques d'Orient (Journal officiel 1870; L'Orient 1877). Month not known.

entries.headline: The Balloon Letter: Egypt remembered under siege
entries.digest: With Paris besieged and letters leaving it by balloon, Ibsen wrote a long verse letter to a Swedish lady recalling his Egyptian journey: the pharaohs' temples, the canal festival, the Empress. He turned the memory into a warning against the new German militarism he saw around him in Dresden.
entries.source_note: GHDI (Ballonbrief, December 1870); University of Oslo chronology (1870).

entries.headline: 120,000 dead: the figure in Nasser's speech
entries.digest: Announcing the nationalisation of the canal company, President Nasser said that 120,000 Egyptians had died digging the canal. The figure became part of the national memory of the corvée. Historians such as Caroline Piquet (CNRS) say no reliable archive supports it, while accepting that losses were heavy; the CNRS account speaks of tens of thousands. The company's own records are partial, and the true number is not known.
entries.source_note: CNRS News (Nasser's 120,000; Piquet: no accurate archives support it; 'tens of thousands'). Speech date from standard histories.

entries.headline: Named at last: the Labor Hall of Honor
entries.digest: Nearly 145 years after Promontory, the US Department of Labor inducted the Chinese railroad workers of the Central Pacific into its Hall of Honor. The same year Stanford's project photographed CP payrolls at the California State Railroad Museum, searching them for names. Descendants took part in the 150th anniversary at Promontory in 2019.
entries.source_note: Stanford project post, March 2014 (payroll imaging at the California State Railroad Museum); Hall of Honor induction and 2019 participation from press coverage, not checked to the day.

claims.claim: Concession granted to cut a maritime canal across the isthmus of Suez, for 99 years from opening
claims.evidence: Hérodote dossier; Lesseps, Lettres, journal et documents

claims.claim: Napoleon III's arbitration ends conscripted Egyptian labour on the canal; Egypt pays the company an indemnity; dredgers and foreign workers take over
claims.evidence: CNRS News (Piquet); standard histories for the month

claims.claim: Central Pacific payroll lists Chinese gangs as 'China Men'; over 3,000 Chinese employed by March–May 1865
claims.evidence: CPRR Payroll No. 158 (Stanford project); Stanford project timeline

claims.claim: Strike by several thousand Chinese workers for $40/month (from $35) and shorter tunnel shifts; ends after about a week without a raise
Congress fixes Promontory Summit as the meeting point after the companies had graded past each other
claims.evidence: Joint resolution of 10 Apr 1869 (cited by NPS cultural landscape report); Dodge memoir

claims.claim: Record: 10 miles 56 feet of track laid by hand in about 12 hours, dawn to dusk
claims.evidence: Stanford project timeline; NPS Chinese Labor and the Iron Road

claims.claim: Last spike at Promontory: 1,084½ miles from Omaha (UP) and 690 miles from Sacramento (CP) per the Salt Lake Telegram; a family compilation in Reed's papers gives 1,186 and 638 miles
claims.evidence: Salt Lake Telegram, 11 May 1869; Reed papers compiler's note (flagged inaccurate by the editors)

claims.claim: First coast-to-coast news by wire of a joined line: the single word 'DONE'
Regular transcontinental passenger service begins on both railroads
claims.evidence: NPS Golden Spike cultural landscape report

claims.claim: UP board questions its construction chiefs over the past year's extraordinary expenditure
Mediterranean and Red Sea waters joined in the canal; about 162 km long, about 8 m deep
Federal commission reports Promontory–Ogden deficiencies of $206,000; actual corrective work later cost over $750,000
claims.evidence: Sen. Exec. Doc. 90, cited in NPS Golden Spike cultural landscape report

claims.claim: Inauguration at Port Said with Muslim and Christian blessings
First ceremonial transit begins: L'Aigle leads about 40 ships from Port Said to Ismailia (Lake Timsah) by evening
claims.evidence: Fondation Napoléon; The Spectator (about forty steamers)

claims.claim: Rival claim: HMS Newport (Cdr George Nares) said to have slipped ahead of L'Aigle in the dark and entered first
claims.evidence: Later naval accounts (Dawlish Chronicles); not checked against logs

claims.claim: Procession reaches Suez, completing the opening transit in four days; the deep-draught frigate Berenguela needed until 17 December
claims.evidence: Riou album (16–20 Nov); Spanish expedition article (Berenguela)

convergences.label: The ten-mile day at Rozel
convergences.note: The record exists in company figures and press boasts; the hundreds of Chinese who did most of the work are counted but not named, while eight Irish rail handlers later were.

convergences.label: Postponement week: rain, unpaid wages and early celebrations
convergences.note: California celebrates on the 8th; the Chinese camp at Victory fights and is settled by Strobridge; the UP's delay, publicly blamed on rain, owed something to workers holding Durant's car for wages.

convergences.label: The last spike at Promontory
convergences.note: Owners see commerce and the road to Asia; the photographers frame engines and handshakes; the press counts miles and bells; the Chinese gang lays the last rail and is cheered privately in Strobridge's car.

convergences.label: The Khedive's guests go up the Nile
convergences.note: Two writers sail to Aswan; the third, his arm broken, watches Cairo from a terrace. The canal is still weeks away.

convergences.label: Port Said: blessings and a ship in the dark
convergences.note: The promoter's triumph, a crown prince's printed diary, and a British survey ship said to have stolen first place overnight.

convergences.label: L'Aigle leads the procession to Ismailia
convergences.note: Order in the line of ships is national rank; the London paper, a day behind and a day wrong, asks about dividends.

convergences.label: The Khedive's ball at Ismailia
convergences.note: Sovereigns at one table in a town that was a labour camp; the fellahin who dug the first channel are nowhere in the picture.

convergences.label: Arrival at Suez; the first verdict in London
convergences.note: Lesseps reaches the Red Sea; The Spectator, writing the same day, doubts the tolls will pay.

ties.note: Rival companies to the last: Dodge pressed for the UP to drive the final spike and lost to Stanford's programme minutes before the ceremony.
Reed built what Dodge located; in August 1869 Reed wrote from Boston that Dodge was expected there as the board examined the year's spending.
Both were Union Army railroad men in the Civil War before working for the UP; Russell photographed Dodge's handshake with Montague at Promontory.
The UP's photographer and the Salt Lake photographer worked the same crowd at Promontory on 10 May, with the CP's Alfred Hart.
Employer and workforce: Stanford's company relied on Chinese labour, broke its 1867 strike by cutting off supplies, and kept it largely out of the ceremony.
Most of what is known of the Chinese crews comes from newspapers that counted them, praised their work and rarely named them.
A copy of the Salt Lake Telegram's account of the ceremony was kept in Reed's papers.
The company's first channel was dug by conscripted fellahin until 1864; Lesseps's published papers treat their labour as a question of supply and compensation.
Both sat at the sovereigns' table at the Khedive's supper in Ismailia on 18 November, as Riou's picture records.
Both were among the writers and artists on the Khedive's Nile expedition from 22 October.
Fellow invited writers on the same programme; Gautier, injured, missed the Nile voyage and the canal that Ibsen saw.
The Spectator reported Lesseps's opening speech on the capitulations and doubted his shareholders' returns.
Ibsen's 1870 Balloon Letter, recalling the canal festival, was a warning against the Prussian militarism whose armies the Crown Prince led against France that year.

threads_out.note: Grenville Dodge was a Union major general who rebuilt railroads for Grant and Sherman, and Andrew J. Russell photographed the US Military Railroad Construction Corps; both took wartime railroad practice west to the Union Pacific.
In Stanley's own telling, James Gordon Bennett's October 1869 commission in Paris sent him first to report the Suez Canal opening and then, eventually, to find Livingstone.

Perry's mission had sought coaling ports for a Pacific steam route to Asia; at Promontory Dodge and Stanford presented the finished railroad as the overland link in that same route to the trade of China and Japan.

Most Central Pacific Chinese workers came from the Pearl River Delta counties of Guangdong, the region most disrupted by the Opium Wars and the turmoil that followed, which pushed emigration across the Pacific.
The canal favoured steamships over sail, since sailing ships could not work the narrow channel, and the second half of its digging was done by steam dredgers after conscripted labour ended in 1864.
